highlights.text: a set of many words with unrelated origins
the form or shape of any created thing
al-Bāriʾ al-Muṣawwir (the Fashioner, the Shaper)
a sound root meaning "to touch something" (mass al-shayʾ)
ṭamatha al-rajulu al-marʾata = "the man touched the woman," i.e. had intercourse with her
"whom no man has touched before them, nor jinn" (Q55:56)
highlights.note: the entry's gloss of the verse

highlights.text: In a line of poetry by ʿAdī, "aw ṭamthi l-ʿaṭan" ("or the ṭamth of the pen/fold")
a single core meaning: the dividing or partitioning of a thing
Every portion of a thing is a baʿḍ ("part/some")
baʿūḍa ("gnat/mosquito," plural baʿūḍ)
Proverb: kallaftanī mukhkha al-baʿūḍ ("you charged me with the marrow of the gnat")
highlights.note: proverb; Ibn Aḥmar, lived into Islam

highlights.text: raʾaytu ghirbānan yatabaʿḍaḍna ("I saw crows...")
One core meaning: "rising, height, elevation."
Qur'an 50:10, "wa-l-nakhla bāsiqāt" ("tall palm-trees"), is glossed simply as ṭawīlāt, "tall ones."
"basaqat al-nakhlah" — the palm grew tall and reached full height (al-Khalīl)
highlights.note: verb of the palm growing tall

highlights.text: splitting/cleaving something so it opens and separates
something being impressive or momentous in scale
falaqa = to split or cleave something
al-falaq = daybreak/dawn, because the darkness is split apart by it
infalaqa = it split open (said of a stone, etc.)
The idiom "so-and-so spoke to me min filqin fihi" means he spoke to me plainly/openly
two base meanings: (1) severance and cutting-off, and (2) binding/tying a thing
the opposite of union or connection
to leave one abode for another
the ḥadīth "Emigrate, and do not merely play at emigrating" urges being truly one of them
the exposure or bareness of a thing's outer surface, with nothing covering it
locusts (well known)
A proverb for something that vanishes untraceably: "I don't know which locust-swarm carried it off"
a thing's going back and forth, part of it over part, and the repeating of a thing
The verb is lajja, yalajju, with the first-person form lajijtu, "I persisted"
The lujj of the sea, or its lujja, is its deepest part (qāmūs)
Zuhayr: "He turns over and over a morsel with half-cooked meat in it; it has gone rank
sits close to the semantic field of gleaming and flashing
also a single plank of a ship's boards (alwāḥ al-safīna)
the heat burned and blackened him, so that he stood out visibly from a distance
A line of verse illustrates it: "I watch for a gleam of Suhayl [Canopus]
one sound root whose core idea is stripping a thing of its outer covering — its rind or the hair growing over it
denote the defiant, overbearing one
is a tall structure
the passing on of something
the opposite of sweetness and pleasantness
marra, yamurru: a thing passed, went on its way
The word marra ("a time", as in "I met him once, twice") is, he explains, just a way of referring to a stretch of time that has gone by
a thing became murr, bitter
firmness/hardness combined with extension and length - something solid that also runs on or reaches far
Imru' al-Qays is cited describing two matnas, firm and plump, as the leopard leans on its forearms
one core meaning: splitting/rending open (shaqq, fatḥ)
makharat al-safīnatu al-māʾa — "the ship makhara'd [cleaved through] the water."
(Mawākhir is the plural form later used in the Qur'an for ships that cut through the sea.)
highlights.note: the entry's note on Qur'anic usage

highlights.text: A cited rajaz verse applies the same image to women racing in a swim
the opening out of something and its spreading
نَشَرْتُ الْكِتَابَ — "I spread open the book,"
"God brought the dead back to life and they revived"
ثُمَّ إِذَا شَاءَ أَنْشَرَهُ ("then, when He wills, He revives him," Q 80:22)
a verse of al-Aʿshā marveling at "the dead man come back to life (al-nāshir)."
this root is a sound one, and it points to beauty, comeliness, and purity/clarity
Al-naḍra means "beauty of color" — a fresh, glowing complexion or hue
Ibn Fāris cites Q75:22: "Faces, that day, radiant" (wujūhun yawma'idhin nāḍira), as the model instance of this sense
the well-known hadith: "May God make radiant a man who heard my words and preserved them"
the half of a thing
a kind of service and being put to use
both mean the half of something
A verse of poetry: "No mudd fed her, nor half a mudd, nor little dates, nor going hungry."
a single core idea: shying away, recoiling, and moving apart
an animal (or anything else) shies and bolts
a band/company of men — also from the same core, because they "rally forth" (yanfirūn) to give aid
لَقِيتُهُ قَبْلَ صَيْحٍ وَنَفْرٍ ("I met him before any cry or bolting") = very early, before anyone cries out or stirs
a single root whose core idea is height and elevation
the she-camel. He offers this as a possible member of the same pattern, the connection being the animal's tall build
"the male camel became like a she-camel." A comparison drawn from the she-camel, used as a proverb
"خَرْقَاءُ ذَاتُ نِيقَةٍ" — "a clumsy woman with fastidious taste."
a sound root with a single core idea: the descending of a thing and its coming down or settling into place
نَزَلَ الْمَطَرُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ نُزُولًا ("the rain came down from the sky")
provisions prepared for a lodger/guest
arranging a thing and setting it in its proper place/rank (manzila)
one core meaning: following something step by step, tracking it
اقْتَصَصْتُ الْأَثَرَ, "I followed the track,"
A story or narration is something followed point by point and then told.
the offender has done to him exactly what he did to the first person, so the retaliation "follows his track."
swift walking — faster than an ordinary gait but short of an outright run (ʿadw)
earnest exertion or striving in some matter
it means the boy grew old enough to pursue and work alongside [his father]
most often saʿy is applied to praiseworthy deeds, citing a verse of poetry
the ritual walking between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa
derives three distinct core meanings for the root س-ح-ل (s-ḥ-l)
sāḥil ("shore," literally an active-participle shape, "one that strips") actually means masḥūl, "a thing stripped" — because the water strips/scours it
cited from a line of Zuhayr's poetry, "of loosely-twisted and tightly-twisted [strands]."
derives this root from the number seven
"seven heavens" (2:29), "seven mighty ones" i.e. the seven heavens (78:16)
Said to be named for the completeness of its strength, seven being one of the "perfect numbers."
A verse by a Hudhalī poet ("as though he were a slave of Abū Rabīʿa's family, musbiʿ") is read two ways
One view: it means Sūrat al-Fātiḥa, since it has seven verses
The Qurʾān's sūras are called al-mathānī ("the repeated") because the narratives are repeated within them
a single core sense: straightness/uprightness
هذا لا يساوي كذا = "this does not equal that"
the middle (of a house, etc.)
Qurʾānic witness: "then he saw him in the midst (sawāʾ) of the Hellfire"
al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line about a serpent that is "no equal (bi-siyy) to you."
"nor did she turn... to any other than you"
وقاه الله كلّ سوء = "God guarded him from every evil"
to guard oneself, take precaution
A cited phrase: "whoever disobeys God, no protectress will guard him from Him."
A verse of al-Namir uses tuqā in this sense of self-guarding heedfulness
Proverb: "the brave man is protected" (الشجاع موقّى)
